query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A combined high‐throughput CALPHAD simulation and precision high‐temperature experimental protocol (using differential scanning calorimetry, dilatometry, and in‐situ high‐temperature X‐ray diffraction) can accurately determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties for single‐phase high‐entropy alloys with an average error below 10%.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic, homogeneous high-entropy alloy (HEA) samples (e.g., single-phase FCC or BCC HEAs) synthesized via conventional cast or additive manufacturing routes.
generation.intervention: Perform high-throughput CALPHAD calculations to predict fusion thermodynamics, then validate and refine these predictions using precision high-temperature experiments (DSC, dilatometry, and in-situ XRD) under controlled inert atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted on HEAs with at least five principal elements; experiments carried out under near-equilibrium conditions in inert or reducing environments to minimize oxidation, with controlled heating rates and well-calibrated instruments.
generation.structural_mediator: Controlled, homogeneous single-phase microstructures that minimize compositional segregation and non-equilibrium effects.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of HEAs leads to predictable trends in fusion properties which can be captured by calibrated thermodynamic (CALPHAD) models; precise experiments serve to refine simulation parameters, thereby ensuring that the integrated approach efficiently yields melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change data with reduced uncertainty.
generation.predicted_outcome: Computed fusion properties from the integrated protocol will match direct experimental measurements within a 10% relative error margin across the compositional space of HEAs.
generation.baseline: Traditional measurements in simpler binary or ternary alloys typically exhibit 10-15% experimental scatter; the integrated protocol aims to reduce this scatter by leveraging high-throughput computational prediction calibrated by state-of-the-art experimental techniques.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be less reliable in HEAs that develop significant microsegregation, compositional inhomogeneity, or metastable phases during melting; if such effects dominate, error margins may exceed the 10% target.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include potential sensitivity to non-equilibrium effects during melting and slight deviations in sample homogeneity which may introduce additional error; also, the modeling of liquid-phase interactions in multi-component systems may require further refinement.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of single-phase HEA compositions; perform independent high-temperature DSC, dilatometry, and in-situ XRD measurements to quantify fusion properties, then compare these experimental values with CALPHAD-based predictions. Ensure a range of heating rates and controlled ambient conditions to minimize extrinsic effects.
measurements: Melting temperature via in-situ high-temperature XRD and DSC
Fusion enthalpy and entropy via calibrated DSC across controlled heating rates
Volume change at melting via high-precision dilatometry
Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties using equilibrium phase analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated approach’s predictions systematically deviate from the directly measured fusion properties by more than 10% for a majority (>50%) of the tested HEA compositions, or if non-equilibrium effects undermine reproducibility, then the proposed method is falsified.

Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system.
